This theory, initially focused on analyzing the properties of geodesics in a space of probability distributions, was later rekindled in the 1980s by Indian mathematician Indian mathematician Indian Rajagopal during this time period,  research on the topic gained significant traction.  By introducing the concept of the optimal transport plan, Indian mathematician Indian Rajagopal successfully applied this theory to the study of population dynamics and biological systems, while later works focused on the application of linear programming techniques.  This paper aims to provide an overview of the current state-of-the-art in computational methods for approximating the solution to the optimal transport problem,  focusing on the use of gradient descent and related first-order optimization techniques.  By detailing the theoretical and algorithmic aspects of the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm,  the work will also examine the use of primal-dual algorithms and other high-performance methods for approximating the solution to the optimal transport problem,  including techniques such as entropic regularization and gradient matching.  This paper will also discuss the use of randomization and other high-performance methods,  such as randomized optimal transport and approximate optimal transport,  in order to improve computational efficiency. Ramanujan, the Indian mathematician, proposed a family of modular equations that have become crucial in modern number theory. He derived these equations using the theta function of a binary quadratic form related to a Hecke group. Surprisingly, it is shown here that his work can be derived as a straightforward consequence of the Hecke group's fundamental properties. Additionally, we present a new proof of one of Ramanujan's identities using the Maass forms of the full modular group, and provide a brief overview of the existing generalization to symplectic groups.

We have conducted a detailed analysis of the Hubble constant using eight gravitationally lensed quasars from the Keck spectroscopic follow-up of the Dark Energy Survey. Our analysis involved observing 31 images of 23 quasars with medium to high resolution over a period of several years with LRIS. We obtained redshift measurements for 27 images and found that four systems feature multiple images with varying redshifts, while four systems feature a lensing galaxy with a redshift significantly higher than the quasar. We also discovered that the velocity variation of the quasars' emission lines is consistent with the velocity difference between the quasars' image and the foreground lens, and in some cases, the velocity difference of a second image is consistent with the velocity difference between the primary image and the foreground lens. We have calculated the time delay for six systems using the time-lens model technique, and in the remaining two systems, we were able to constrain the time delay within a specific range. Our analysis also involved a comparison of the lensing galaxy redshift measurements from Keck with those obtained by the Dark Energy Survey. We found that the discrepancy between the two datasets is significantly reduced, and the difference is no longer statistically significant. We then used the lensing galaxy redshift measurements to constrain the lensing galaxy's mass and the time delay of the quasars. Our analysis revealed that the lensing galaxy's mass is consistent with the predictions of the MOSES semi-analy

The goal of this article is to examine the prior solutions to the nonlinear q-fractional differential equations over time scales, with a focus on uncovering the underlying principles. Through an exhaustive analysis, the work presents a novel approach that integrates a time scale iteration method and fixed point theory to solve the mentioned equations. The results were validated through the use of numerical examples, which demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed method. Additionally, the article compares and contrasts this approach with existing solutions to the problem.

Theoretical analysis confirms that phonons exhibit the topological phonon Hall effect provided certain conditions are met: 1) the Hamiltonian must change by an integer factor from one Brillouin zone point to another, 2) the Hamiltonian must differ in at least one direction from a single point in the Brillouin zone, and 3) the Hamiltonian must exhibit a specific property at this point. This theory is validated through numerical simulations of a harmonic crystal with varying layers and by applying it to the 2D hexagonal lattice of graphene, which experimentally confirmed the existence of a topological phonon Hall effect.

Raman spectroscopy has become a versatile tool in biochemistry and biophysics due to its ability to analyze multiple samples efficiently. Despite this, achieving high-resolution Raman spectra of broad samples has been a significant challenge. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel method, based on the Nod and Shuffle technique, that enables the acquisition of high-quality Raman spectra from large areas by selectively exciting specific points on a sample and measuring the resulting emissions. This approach is particularly useful for studying biological samples, where it can detect subtle changes in the presence of certain molecules by utilizing a Raman technique called SERDS. To further enhance this capability, we have integrated our method with a Raman microscope, allowing for the rapid acquisition and analysis of spectral images. This state-of-the-art technology has been successfully demonstrated in both spectral imaging and spectral imaging microscopy, showcasing its potential for analyzing large biological samples with great precision.

The Fejér and Stieglitz inequalities, along with their Levin form, have been extended to the complex Herglotz-Riesz space through a natural matrix generalization. In this study, we examine and establish a unified framework for these inequalities, along with their inverse forms, within the context of operator matrices that take values in Banach spaces over the complex plane.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for an observer watching a black hole evaporate, starting with the Schwarzschild and Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker cosmological black hole. We find that the mean null energy density is initially negative but becomes positive as the horizon evaporates for the Schwarzschild black hole under certain conditions. In contrast, the mean null energy density remains positive throughout the evaporation process in the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker cosmological black hole. Additionally, we examine the mean null energy density for an AdS black hole undergoing island formation due to the presence of a boundary. In this case, we find that the mean null energy density is initially negative but increases to a positive value as the horizon evaporates, provided the region outside the island is the dominant effective horizon.

In this presentation, we examine how CFT operators are mirrored in lattice structures, leading to emergent dimensions that can be described through lattice-based free field representations. It's found that the lattice's continuous dimensions align with the discrete dimensions of the CFT operator space, with the relationship also applicable to higher-order operators. This connection is further explored in relation to chiral and non-chiral theories, their respective dimensions, and the Gliozzi-Kokshen-Solitro dimensions.

Industry cyber security issues are a pressing concern in environments where physical processes are critical to production and operations. As a result, developing robust cyber security measures for industrial control systems (ICSs) is a top priority. This requires a comprehensive approach to addressing vulnerability issues, and establishing a universal framework for assessing progress in this regard can help facilitate this goal. A new model, the ICS-CTM2, has been developed to evaluate the cyber security testing capabilities of organizations responsible for ICSs. This model outlines the procedures necessary for conducting effective testing on these systems and outlines key characteristics that need to be considered during the testing process.

In complex environments with multiple agents, developing an optimal learning strategy is a significant challenge. To address this, we present a new approach called Greedy-based Worth Representation for Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (GW-MARL), designed to improve cooperation among self-interested agents. By leveraging Q-learning and the greedy approach, GW-MARL evaluates actions based on their potential individual benefits and assigns higher value to more beneficial actions, thereby increasing the agent's cooperation. The worth of each action is represented as a vector space, allowing for a multi-objective decision-making mechanism. This approach can be applied to both fully and partially connected agents, and is robust against noisy observations. Notably, our method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in the Sticky Mixtures problem.

A common stereotype is defined as an exaggerated and false idea about a specific group, intended to justify a particular action or decision and usually based on the stereotype rather than the actual characteristics of the group. This phenomenon has significant implications for pre-trained language models, which are often trained on data containing biased information. This study investigates the presence of stereotypes in pre-trained language models, specifically focusing on a set of predefined stereotypes developed by the US National Science Foundation. We evaluated two prominent models, BERT and RoBERTa, and assessed their performance in identifying and making accurate statements about individuals from various social groups, including women, African Americans, and University of California students. We also compared the models' performance to a control model that uses meta-information to make predictions. The results show that both models performed poorly in recognizing stereotypes and often relied on the target's identity rather than the accuracy of the statement. These findings have important implications for the ethics of language modeling and the need to address and correct the biases present in pre-trained models.

To minimize power losses in electric distribution networks, optimal electrical tilt optimization requires continuous adjustment of tilt factors. However, this is challenging due to the lack of accurate distribution network data, particularly on customer-side voltages and currents, which are often concealed, and the difficulty in collecting or purchasing measurement data from across large-scale systems. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel off-policy learning approach that utilizes available distribution network data, learning customer loads and transformer voltages to determine the optimal tilt settings. This approach leverages a deep neural network to estimate tilt adjustments based on a novel off-policy loss function. Experimental results based on the IEEE 123-bus system demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reducing power losses in comparison to other approaches.

A comprehensive update on determining the CKM angle gamma through LHCb experiments is presented, utilizing data collected at 7, 8, and 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 5.8 inverse femtobarns. A combination of six pirel-based studies, incorporating various hadronic final states, yields an estimated gamma value. Our measurement reveals gamma to reside in the 45.3 degrees to 56.6 degrees range at the 1 standard deviation level, and the result, at 53.6 degrees with a 17.2 degree margin of error (statistical: 3.1 degree, systematic: 0.6 degree, life-time influenced systematic: 0.2 degree, pirel-related systematic: 0.2 degree], differs from the current World Average by 0.4 degree and exhibits a 0.3 standard deviation significance level.

This note delves into the geometric properties of a particular class of second-order ellipsoidal functions, specifically their relationship with complex conjugate pairs. We investigate the symmetry constraints imposed by these functions, resulting in a unique set of conic sections on the space of self-adjoint operators. Additionally, our analysis expands the scope of application for a well-established theorem in the field, originally derived for real variables, to encompass complex variables. We provide illustrative examples to demonstrate the distinct geometric characteristics of these ellipsoids.

A data marketplace facilitates an exchange of personal information for rewards, utilizing an incentive mechanism to ensure participants act in the market's best interest. The market's efficiency in allocating rewards to participants is influenced by the data seller's preferences. A data market is beneficial as it enables data subjects to receive compensation for their data and facilitates data users at a lower cost. To understand the market's efficiency under various data seller preferences, a data market simulation was conducted with two participant groups. The data seller preferences were explored through a survey and the data market simulation revealed that data sellers prioritize rewards over, or in conjunction with, other factors such as privacy and data protection when motivated by financial incentives. The data market simulation also revealed that participants who highly value data privacy were unlikely to participate in the market.

In 5G and beyond 5G networks, Quicker-than-Nyquist (QTN) signaling is gaining interest for improved spectral efficiency, despite its reduced detection reliability compared to traditional modulation schemes. This study introduces a deep learning-based list sphere decoding (DL-LSD) method to address the detection challenges of QTN-signals. The approach is applied to binary phase shift keying (BPSK) QTN-signals, which are created by arranging QTN-codewords into a low-density parity-check (LDPC) code to ensure reliable transmission. The proposed DL-LSD method is then used to detect the QTN-signals, yielding a significant error rate reduction of approximately 10 dB compared to a maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoder.

This article explores order topology and the Frink ideal structure within effect algebras. Initially, we demonstrate how the order topology of an effect algebra is defined by its finest measure-theoretic topology. Additionally, we establish that in effect algebras with a Riesz decomposition property in the order topology, specific elements are distinct. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in such effect algebras, subeffects and subgroups can be generated from the resolution on the associated lattice of effect subalgebras. Finally, we examine the connection between the Frink ideal structure and the order structure of such effect algebras, showing that in effect algebras with a RDP in the order topology, every element forms the supremum of a Frink ideal and a Frink subgroup.

Recent studies have demonstrated that self-supervised learning's data augmentation regularizer can improve model performance on various tasks. A key component in this regularizer is the selection of samples for augmentation, which can significantly impact model performance. Traditionally, these samples are chosen randomly, but we propose a more informed approach by selecting samples based on their saliency maps. We introduce SaliencyMix, a data augmentation regularizer that identifies and augments the most influential input features for each task. Through comprehensive experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10, SaliencyMix has been shown to outperform existing state-of-the-art regularizers, underscoring the importance of saliency-based sample selection in enhancing model performance.

Let $\mathcal{U}$ be the infinite-dimensional Iwahori--Hecke algebra over a non-integer, non-torsion algebraically closed field $k$. In a prior paper, a specific basis was used to describe $\mathcal{U}$, and then traces were defined and analyzed. These traces, however, do not align with standard expectations within the realm of quantum groups. Notably, they do not adhere to the usual properties associated with roots and weights. Furthermore, they do not correspond with the trace function linked to an infinite-dimensional quantum group. An examination of the central extensions linked to $\mathcal{U}$ reveals that the center's behavior deviates from typical patterns. An isomorphism exists between the character space of $\mathcal{U}$ and the ring formed by polynomials in a specific variable, with no apparent connection to the quantum group's root system or weights.

A novel, yet untested, gravitational theory, which adheres to general relativity and is stable, has been proposed. This theory, which extends Horndeski's action, can be distinguished from other theories by the presence of two new, independent dimensionless parameters. These parameters, denoted as $\xi$ and $\xi'$, have significant implications, as they can either align with established cosmological principles or lead to an altered understanding of the universe's evolution. Research suggests that the introduction of $\xi$ and $\xi'$ may be responsible for the observed tension between the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure data. To further investigate this theory, a new method has been developed to estimate the value of $\xi$ and $\xi'$ using birefringence effects in galaxy alignments. This method, which combines data from the cosmic shear and intrinsic galaxy alignment (GIHA) surveys, has the potential to provide a more accurate understanding of these parameters. Furthermore, this approach can be used to determine the value of $\xi$ and $\xi'$ with a precision of approximately 0.1, allowing scientists to make more accurate predictions about the universe's evolution.

We investigate the unusual rheological properties of discrete particle systems, such as those made of microgel particles or stiff fibers, to understand the interactions between confinement and non-conventional rheology. Through numerical simulations, we examine the effects of confinement on the viscoelastic properties of free particles and particles trapped in a periodic pattern. We discover that when particles are tightly packed, confinement leads to an increase in elasticity and a decrease in viscosity, resulting in a negative ratio of these two properties. This behavior is unique to systems of free particles and is not observed in systems of confined particles, where the ratio is positive. We analyze the impact of confinement on the mechanical response of these systems, revealing a significant role for stress transmission between particles. The findings suggest that confinement of soft particles could enable the creation of materials with enhanced elasticity.

The self-extraction of gold nanoparticles from a polymer solution under near-infrared light illumination holds great promise for applications such as cancer treatment and optical data storage. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers employed a combination of computer simulations and machine learning to predict how the particles melt and interact. By using a machine learning model to analyze experimental data, the team was able to create a model that accurately simulated the particles melting and confirmed that a high temperature at the particle surface is responsible for their disintegration. The results also suggested that a significant increase in the particles' volume over time, caused by the melting, is responsible for their physical breakdown.

This is the initial part of a study that develops parameterized versions of known mathematical theorems in the field of dynamical systems. The initial section of this paper establishes a theoretical framework, drawing from previous work, and presents a generalized form of the well-known Borsuk Antipodes Theorem. The second section will apply this new theorem to understand dynamical system behavior. The initial section also explores specific conditions that can be added to the main theorem to examine spaces of mappings that have a particular level of complexity. The research then delves into a more comprehensive theory of specific mathematical operations known as Brouwer's and Ljusternik-Sobolev functions.

The concept of taste tasting involves a complex process of chemical breakdown and molecular identification within the taste buds, resulting in distinct sensations. Various taste patterns have been developed to categorize the diverse range of flavors, yet a universal system remains to be discovered. Our investigation into taste patterns involved applying graph theory to create a universal encoding system, translating taste descriptions to nodes and expressing their connections through edges. Our analysis of 77 taste patterns, including culinary terms and taste theories, revealed relationships between them. Our research led to the creation of three taste trees, each presenting a unique perspective on the complex interplay of taste. The first tree highlights the hierarchical nature of taste, while the second and third emphasize the parallel and network aspects of taste connections, respectively. This research aims to provide a comprehensive and flexible framework for understanding the intricate system of tastes.

We obtain new, closed-form expressions for the (h;q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials with a beta function contribution. The mentioned identities arise from an innovative application of the q-beta integration technique on the q-WZ pair. Additionally, we derive the q versions of the Bernoulli polynomials that contribute to the corresponding beta functions.

In cases where covariate balance is uncertain, observational studies are often used to estimate the effects of treatments.  However, there's been a lack of research on methods to assess potential covariate imbalance.  We've developed a new method combining reinforcement learning to accurately model the treatment assignment process and estimate potential imbalance.  Our approach can be applied to various scenarios, including continuous, binary, and ordinal variables, and can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of covariate balancing techniques.  We've also conducted a simulation study to compare the performance of our method with existing approaches and found that it provides more accurate and detailed information about covariate imbalance.  Furthermore, our method can be used to assess the potential long-term effects of treatments, allowing us to make more informed decisions about covariate balancing and provide a clearer understanding of treatment effects.

In a case-control study, participants are selected based on a specific outcome, and researchers aim to identify potential causes of this outcome by analyzing exposures and other factors. However, the recruitment process can introduce a memory bias that disproportionately affects cases, leading to a phenomenon known as the recall and selection bias. Although some studies have addressed this bias at a general level, a clear method for accounting for recall and selection bias in case-control studies is lacking. This study proposes a causal modeling framework to address recall and selection bias, starting with a model that estimates the probability of exposure based on covariates. A subsequent model is used to estimate the direct causal effect of exposure on health, while the recalled and selected counterfactuals are simulated to correct for memory bias. This approach is validated through simulations and applied to a real-world study of a French cohort of individuals who were exposed to a chemical called di-isocyanate.

Generative models can be divided into two categories, generative and autoencoder architectures. While generative models can produce new data, they are limited to unsupervised learning and don't account for data's inherent missing information. In contrast, autoencoder architectures are suitable for supervised learning but can only generate the encoded representations. A common approach to address this issue is to train generative models on encoded representations, a method known as a autoencoder. However, a major drawback of this approach is that the unsupervised learning of generative models doesn't align with the supervised learning of the autoencoder, which leads to a discrepancy in the estimated statistics of the latent space. A recent study has shown that the maximum likelihood training of generative models and autoencoders is inconsistent. A new approach has been proposed to address this discrepancy by using reversible layers, which can learn and invert the joint and conditional distributions of the data and its latent space. This method has been tested on various datasets and has shown that it successfully closes the gap between generative models and autoencoders, resulting in better performance compared to previous methods.

The concept of "smart city" analytics involves time-series data analysis to enable informed decision-making by city administrators. To achieve this, a substantial data set is collected and processed, often involving the calculation of various indicators. However, the sheer volume of data makes it impractical to display all information, so a selected subset of the most significant indicators is typically used for visualization. Our research introduces a novel data analysis method that leverages visualization to examine the interconnections among various chosen indicators. This approach allows for the discovery of patterns where attribute correlations deviate from those expected in independent random data, thereby facilitating more effective city data evaluation.

This research explores the development of geometric multigrid methods as preconditioners for two types of finite element systems derived from the reaction-diffusion equation and the generalized Stokes equations. The systems in question utilize the HDG-P0 finite element method with specialized bilinear forms tailored to meet the linear systems' ill-conditioning. The resulting system matrices, denoted as A and A*, feature mass scaling and a condition number of approximately O (ε^{-1}). Building upon previous work, this study extends the research by incorporating more general HDG-formulations, expanding the class of finite element pairs that can be optimized, and enhancing the multigrid preconditioner with dynamic Vanka coarsening and dynamic smoothing strategies. The findings indicate that the proposed multigrid preconditioners achieve superior performance, particularly for smaller values of ε, compared to other standard preconditioning techniques.

Missingness in data analysis can lead to biased results. To address this issue, researchers investigate the sensitivity of data analysis techniques to missing data assumptions. A widely discussed metric for evaluating this sensitivity in observational studies is the E-value, which quantifies the impact of alternative assumptions on findings. Our research aims to adapt this E-value framework for Bayesian missing data methods, specifically for assessing sensitivity in Bayesian missing data analyses. To achieve this, we develop an E-value for Bayesian missing data analyses by treating different assumptions as competing hypotheses and deriving the posterior probabilities of these alternatives. Additionally, we introduce a novel sensitivity metric, the Bayesian sensitivity ratio, to gauge the robustness of Bayesian findings compared to frequentist approaches, and we illustrate the application of this framework with a case study involving a Bayesian meta-analysis.

In crossover trials, missing data are common, and several approaches have been proposed to handle it. Building upon previous research, this study extends the existing theory to multivariate crossover trials. The study develops probability-based methods for estimating treatment effects that take into consideration the probability of missing data, as well as multiple endpoints. The accuracy of these new methods is demonstrated through a simulation and confirmed in an actual clinical trial.

This article builds on the concept of a weak monoidal framework, a category-based framework initially introduced in the arXon category theory framework. We develop a novel category called CWMF (CW-hypergroupoid of weak monoidal frameworks), and demonstrate the efficacy of this new framework by proving it generates a coherent CW structure, specifically the CW structure of the associahedra series associated with CWMF.

The growing interest in in-memory computing has led to a surge in the development of in-drift functionalities, such as machine learning and graph processing. To address the need for in-drift functionalities, this research introduces CODIC, an innovative system that leverages DRAM to implement custom logic circuits. By utilizing a unique combination of DRAM's row activation and column access control signals, CODIC enables the creation of small, flexible logic circuits. To optimize performance, CODIC employs a hybrid approach that combines logic computation with DRAM access. The efficacy of CODIC is demonstrated through simulations and practical implementations, showcasing its ability to deliver high performance and energy efficiency. Furthermore, CODIC's design is adaptable, as evidenced by its ability to achieve a 14% improvement in ML accuracy for a specific application by integrating a custom logic function into the DRAM.

This research paper is the second installment in a series exploring the role of functional programming in managing and coordinating virtual network resources. It delves into the role of programming in network evolution, presenting innovative approaches to designing networks through a lens grounded in functional composition. By drawing on category theory, the paper demonstrates how virtual networks can be perceived as products resulting from the combination of independent components. Building on this perspective, the authors propose a new model for virtual network design, where resources are integrated and customized to suit specific network requirements. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, the authors present a proof-of-concept implementation based on OpenDaylight's Java API and further discuss potential performance optimizations.

To investigate the behavior of a variety of multi-qubit gates in the context of the toric code's phase-flip code, we examine the impact of stabilizer errors on the application of a single or multiple error correction cycles. This is done using an analytical approach to calculate the time required for errors to accumulate and propagate, as well as a numerical method that simulates the behavior of a system in a higher-dimensional space. The results show that, when multiple gates are applied, the rate of stabilizer errors accelerates, eventually causing the code to fail sooner than if individual gates are used. This suggests that using a high frequency of stabilizer gates may improve performance.

A universal system for managing observatory tasks can be particularly useful for coordinating complex, multi-site research projects. This system would be crucial in executing large-scale projects that involve distributed astronomy, where a single researcher may hold expertise on multiple sites. Existing systems for task management, although effective in the observatory setting, are designed with a specific site in mind and are not adaptable to diverse locations. To address this issue, we're developing OPUS - a task management system based on the standards set by the International Virtual Observatory Organization - with the goal of achieving full interoperability with existing facilities. As a result, it can operate with a high degree of autonomy, requiring minimal assistance from the user. We outline the design and initial implementation of OPUS, highlighting its ability to execute tasks at the NRC's HSTRO - the 4K-resolution infrared camera located at the CFHT.

This research proposes an innovative approach to teaching fundamental concepts of complex wireless networks through an interactive simulation. Leveraging digital game-driven learning, a virtual simulation was created to model the behavior of IEEE 802.11 wireless networks, allowing students to set and adjust the simulation's parameters and observe the resulting network dynamics. As students make adjustments, the simulation tracks their decisions and presents the simulation's outcomes in a manner that fosters self-reflection. Initially evaluated by a small group of graduate and undergraduate students, the simulation yielded encouraging results, indicating that this method effectively facilitates the education of IEEE 802.11 wireless networks, enhances student engagement, and aligns with students' preferences for digital learning tools.

The ozone layer's relationship with oxygen is crucial for understanding paleoclimatology and paleo-atmospheric studies, but modeling this relationship poses a challenge due to its reliance on complex chemistry and limited observational records. Aiming to improve our understanding of Earth's past environments and facilitate comparisons with other planets' atmospheres, we created a model that simulates the O2-O3 relationship across a wide range of atmospheric conditions. The results show that the O2-O3 relation is influenced by atmospheric chemistry, particularly during low O2 and high O3 phases, but remains relatively consistent across a range of planetary parameters, temperature, and chemical reactions. These findings suggest that ozone may serve as a proxy for oxygen in a variety of planetary contexts, but its relation is most reliable when O2 is high and O3 is low. Future research could improve the accuracy of this relation, particularly in low O2 and high O3 scenarios, by incorporating more precise measurements and observations.

The quantum Hall effect's two-dimensional manifestation in a Hall bar is a long-standing concept, yet three-dimensional systems exhibit unique and unexplored properties. In this study, we investigate the Hofstadter model's three-dimensional variant, where a periodic potential is applied in one direction and a small bias is applied perpendicular to it. In this setup, we find that a steady surface current is generated at the boundary, characterized by a quantized current density varying with time. The time dependence of this phenomenon is uncovered, revealing that the surface current is a result of chiral modes interacting with topological states. The interaction between these modes produces a non-equilibrium state, where the surface current is stabilized even in the absence of an external magnetic field. The 3D Hofstadter model's behavior is further validated by comparing it to a more realistic model of a 4HgTe quantum well, where we demonstrate the stability of surface currents under realistic conditions.

Recent advancements in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have led to improved translation quality compared to traditional Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) methods. Despite this progress, NMT still struggles with translating specialized domains, such as medicine, where the use of multilingual models with multiple source languages can be problematic. This is due to a significant knowledge gap in low-resource languages, which negatively affects the model's performance. To overcome these challenges, our proposed solution involves creating a specialized medical translation model by fine-tuning a multilingual NMT model on a specific dataset. This fine-tuned model is then used for fine-grained domain adaptation, translating words from a source language to multiple target languages within the medical domain. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms traditional methods and achieves notable improvements in translation quality, particularly when evaluating specific medical terms.

A system consisting of nonthermal electrons, warm ions, and positively charged dust grains is examined to investigate the formation of altered-ion-acoustic waves. The use of a two-fluid model and a set of reduced equations allows for a qualitative analysis of the impact of various physical parameters on the properties of AIAW waves. Numerical solutions of a set of ambipolar equations confirm the theoretical findings and reveal the conditions necessary for the formation of AIAW solitary and shock waves. Interestingly, these parameters have a complex effect, with certain factors promoting the stability of AIAWs while others do not. Additionally, certain conditions lead to the formation of AIAWs that are more compressive and stable than those formed under other physical conditions.

This research presents a novel approach to unsupervised sentence representation 
pretraining for multi-lingual information retrieval, focusing on improving 
cross-lingual and in-lingual sentence similarity for better retrieval outcomes. 
The proposed method employs a pretraining objective that promotes context-aware 
sentence representation through the utilization of randomly swapped sentence pairs 
within the same language or between languages, alongside an encoding objective 
utilizing masked language modeling. By integrating a dense representation and 
linguistic information, our approach enhances in-lingual and cross-lingual 
similarity. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms other 
methods in English and non-English languages on a range of tasks, including 
sentence similarity and query relevance. Moreover, our approach achieves 
state-of-the-art results on a multilingual retrieval task, as evaluated by the 
DUC 2003 English benchmark, without any need for cross-lingual parallel data.

Multimodal learning, which combines information from various sources, is an area of research that aims to improve performance by combining modalities. Prototypical networks have achieved notable success in this field, but often treat different modalities as separate entities, failing to effectively combine them. This work proposes a new framework, PMR, which addresses this limitation by introducing a Prototypical Modal Adjustment method that can be applied to any prototypical network. PMR achieves this by first identifying the most similar prototypical representation of a given sample and then using the prototypical representation with the highest similarity to adjust the input sample. This process is repeated until convergence to avoid the input bias caused by the initial prototypical representations. The proposed method is tested on various classification tasks and demonstrates improved performance. Additionally, PMR is applied to a specific task, a two-sample based class-inference task, and achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by the experiments conducted on a specific dataset.

The standard theory of particle transport, encompassing diffusion, convection, and dispersion as well as the Grad-Shafranov equation for fluids, is expanded by incorporating the effects of vector resonance domination. This extension leads to the introduction of the "vector enhancement factor" and results in the development of a new fluid model incorporating the effects of the firehose instability.

This research introduces a new method for generating tensor-based models, which are utilized in various applications such as speech processing and computer vision. Our findings indicate that when initial data is structured in a particular way, these models can effectively approximate more traditional neural network designs. To demonstrate this, we employed a tensor-based network to interpret spoken commands from the Alexa Skills Kit, which we compared to two established neural network architectures: a 1D convolutional neural network, and a fully connected multilayer perceptron. Our experimental results show that these tensor-based networks can effectively match the performance of these more traditional models.

The theory of open quantum systems is a crucial tool for comprehending natural phenomena at a microscopic level. A notable example is the evolution of a two-level atom's excited state probability over time, which is influenced by an external laser field and interactions with a vacuum field. When analyzed using the standard quantum master equation, this process generates stochastic trajectories, known as quantum jumps, that contrast with those derived from an alternative master equation form. This analysis delves into the underlying mathematical structures and compares the resulting probability distributions and stochastic trajectories in both scenarios.

This study explores the geometric influence of plasmonic aluminum (Al) nanoparticles on light absorption in silicon thin-film solar cells. The research involves designing and simulating square, triangular, and circular Al nanoparticles on p-type silicon thin-film solar cells. The performance of these solar cells is assessed using the SCAPS program, which evaluates the impact of these nanoparticles on device efficiency. Our findings indicate that silicon thin-film solar cells incorporating plasmonic aluminum nanoparticles can achieve higher energy conversion efficiency. Specifically, we discovered that these solar cells experienced efficiency increases of 0.16%, 0.19%, 0.19%, 0.20%, and 0.21% for triangular, circular, square, square with a 0.1 $\mu$m gap, and square with a 0.2 $\mu$m gap nanoparticles, respectively. The results suggest that circular nanoparticles yield the best outcome, followed by square with a 0.2 $\mu$m gap and triangular shapes.

The study of computational complexity within descriptive complexity theory has been ongoing since the 1980s. The focus has centered around understanding the relationship between different models, particularly with regards to their capacity to solve problems that are typically associated with PTIME. Notably, this includes examining the capabilities of logic-based systems through their ability to express either the truth of a statement or the non-truth of a statement. However, this approach presents a limitation, as it requires the use of existential or universal quantifiers to achieve this. As a result, researchers have explored the use of choice and negation operators to determine if a better understanding of the computational complexity can be achieved. The current study aims to provide an answer to this question by examining the computational capabilities of first-order logic and its variants. The study begins by analyzing the properties of the logic as a complexity class, as proposed by Freyd, and examining the computational capabilities of the systems when the models are restricted. The study then explores the capabilities of the systems when the models are allowed, with particular attention to the use of enumeration constructs. The study shows that the systems are capable of solving PTIME problems when the models are allowed, but only if the models are restricted. The study also demonstrates that the systems are capable of solving PTIME problems when the models are allowed, but only if the models are restricted.

LSTM networks have become a leading deep learning method for NLP and image processing, but their high power consumption makes them less suitable for deployment on small devices. To overcome this limitation, a new framework is introduced that optimizes the execution of LSTM networks on video datasets using advanced tensor decomposition and a co-design approach. By applying HT decomposition and a co-design framework, significant energy and memory savings are achieved on FPGA platforms. In particular, a 42.1% reduction in energy consumption and 34.2% reduction in memory usage are demonstrated on an Xilinx ZCU102 board. This innovative approach offers a new path for integrating LSTM networks on various platforms while minimizing their energy consumption.

The MAVLink protocol, used by the Ardupilot and PX4 projects, has become a standard communication method for unmanned aerial systems (UAS). Despite its widespread use, security vulnerabilities in the protocol have been identified by security researchers. These flaws make UAS susceptible to attacks, compromising their safety and posing significant risks. To address these concerns, we first examined the security weaknesses in the MAVLink protocol, revealing 14 distinct vulnerabilities. To enhance safety, we proposed a secure message exchange protocol, utilizing encryption and other measures, to protect UAS from unauthorized access. Our solution was successfully implemented and tested on a quadrotor UAS, providing positive results.

The rapid growth of distributed systems and ad-hoc networks has led to a significant increase in the need for rapid network reconfigurations. However, current network emulators lack the ability to dynamically create and alter complex topologies in real-time. This limitation hinders the evaluation and optimization of protocols designed for dynamic networks. To address this issue, a new tool called Kollaps was designed. Kollaps is a user-friendly, distributed, and dynamic network emulator that can efficiently replicate the behavior of diverse network architectures, including traditional and distributed systems. It achieves this by leveraging existing network simulators such as Netemf and emulating a range of network protocols. Kollaps is highly adaptable and can be easily extended to support new network emulations based on its modular design. The tool is available as an open-source package, and its source code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/NetLab-AS/kollaps.

The mathematical representation of twistor space can capture the essence of complex spacetime phenomena, such as gravitational waves, by providing an abstract, coordinate-independent model. The non-linear interaction of electromagnetic fields with gravitational forces is a notable example of this phenomenon, and can be effectively analyzed using an enhanced understanding of twistor space. By employing this method, it is possible to gain a more comprehensive and intuitive understanding of the nonlinear effects of gravitation on electromagnetic fields, and can be used to derive a specific mathematical equation describing the nonlinear behavior. The derived equation can be used to gain a deeper understanding of spacetime's complex structures and the interactions that take place, and can be used to provide a more concrete and practical solution to the problem of the nonlinear interaction of electromagnetic and gravitational fields.

Researchers have developed a novel muon detector designed for underground structure imaging using low-energy neutrons. This detector leverages the muon's ionizing potential, allowing it to serve as a localized probe for the underground environment. Composed of two perpendicular layers of plastic scintillator bars and read out with photomultiplier tubes, the detector can distinguish muon hits and track their directions. Optimized for efficient detection, the detector's design prioritizes the highest muon detection efficiency within a 30 degree angular acceptance. Preliminary results from a test setup are presented, accompanied by simulated analysis techniques for simulating muon tracks and calculating the angular resolution.

This is the second edition of the Parsing Expression Parser LL (PELL). This edition expands upon the original PELL (available at github.com/llsif/llp) by incorporating significant features such as support for defined symbols, automated generation of a lexing component, and a more intuitive syntax, designed to be easier to understand and write. A comprehensive tutorial, available at pelly.org, has been revised to accommodate the new features of PELL and ensures smooth integration.

We have investigated how vacuum Cherenkov radiation is influenced by a temperature effect within a specific theoretical model that combines a photon field with spatial confinement.  The study revealed that the process of radiation becomes more unstable as temperature increases, and this instability is directly proportional to the square of the spatial confinement.  Additionally, for weaker interactions, we derived an approximate formula for the rate of radiation, incorporating temperature, and found that it can be expressed through an integral of the Riemann zeta function.

To study the evolution of language forecasts, we developed an approach leveraging large-scale pre-trained language models, allowing us to accurately predict the performance of human experts over complex NLP tasks. By fine-tuning the GPT-2 model and evaluating it on tasks with varying levels of difficulty, we observed that it consistently outperforms human experts across the board. Furthermore, we found that the performance gap between the model and humans is narrower on harder tasks, with results indicating a more nuanced relationship between human and artificial intelligence performance on these tasks. Additionally, we found that the linguistic patterns associated with poor performance are more complex in harder tasks, with a stronger correlation between linguistic features and task difficulty in these cases. Overall, our findings suggest that the language models provide a useful framework for exploring and understanding the predictions and intuitions of human experts in NLP.

We propose a straightforward yet effective approach to determine the three-dimensional pose of an object within a two-dimensional space. Our method relies on a straightforward concept: when an object's pose changes, its turntable movements become visible. To model these transformations, we utilize a learnable non-rigid shape model, which we estimate from an initial static image. We then apply this model to sequential images to calculate the object's motion and pose. Our approach yields accurate pose estimations without requiring a predefined model or extensive training data. Moreover, it can be applied across multiple object categories, even those without prior knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this simple yet powerful method, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and adaptability to novel objects.

In this investigation, we demonstrate the manipulation of the crossed Andreev reflection and its relation to the elastic reflection at an Andreev bound state interface. The interface between two quantum dots and an s-wave superconductor exhibits a specific type of hybridization gap when the energy levels of the dots do not match the superconductor's gap edges. Additionally, when the chemical potential is non-integer times the superconducting gap, significant correlations between the flux-dependent currents caused by the crossed Andreev reflection and the elastic reflection mediated by the Andreev bound state are observed. The dynamic behavior of the ABR current can be controlled by varying the superconducting phase, which also influences the reflection of the ABR current. This unique manipulation has the potential to be applied in quantum bit operations and quantum information processing.

A novel kinetic simulation model has been developed, accounting for the random change in particle orientation that occurs during magnetic reconnection. This model incorporates a more realistic, anisotropic particle distribution, where the z-component of particle velocity is affected by a Gaussian random function. The results show that this anisotropic model accurately replicates the key characteristics of reconnection, including the formation of magnetic islands, the acceleration of electrons, and the resulting electron acceleration spectra. This simulation model may be useful in modeling high-energy phenomena in various physical systems, such as solar flares, gamma-ray bursts, and relativistic astrophysical phenomena.

We explore the production of a Higgs boson along with a $Z$-boson within the framework of the Standard Model and several extensions containing additional scalar fields. The two complex extensions of the Higgs sector we examine include the complex triplet and complex singlet theories. The analysis reveals that high-precision measurements of the Higgs coupling to \(Z$-bosons and transverse momentum of Higgs boson pairs can effectively differentiate between the complex triplet and complex singlet, which are otherwise indistinguishable in the Standard Model. The search for extended scalar sectors can also be effectively conducted using the high-luminosity LHC running at the Higgs boson production threshold.

This paper presents an alternative definition of the combined numerical range's subdifferential, building on previous work from M. Lin and Y. M. Lin. Our definition aligns with the alternative definition of the numerical range's subdifferential as outlined in L. F. Cabral et al.'s study, and it is shown to be consistent with the original definition as proposed by K. Veseli\'c and M. Voigt.

The concept of differential privacy has gained significant attention in recent years, primarily due to its potential to transform sensitive data into anonymized information that does not compromise data security. In the financial sector, the challenge lies in providing detailed market analysis while maintaining strict data protection measures. This study delves into the practical applications of differential privacy within the financial domain, investigating its potential to address the intricate challenges of data anonymization while ensuring the protection of sensitive information.

Key Financial Applications of Differential privacy: 
1. Trading signals, 
2. Portfolio returns, 
3. Market analysis, 
4. Personalized investment advice, 
5. Financial data protection.

In this context, the primary objective is to translate raw financial data into a secure format that does not expose sensitive information, while also addressing the complexities of differential privacy, including the trade-off between privacy and data utility preservation.

This study introduces a novel stochastic process that generates a random dispersion field with a correlation function defined by a specific Gaussian kernel, offering a more comprehensive framework than initially proposed. The original process's limitations are overcome by developing an alternative representation, which facilitates the derivation of a Gaussian-based correlation function for the enhanced stochastic process. The resulting function, determined by a single shape parameter, enables the creation of a random dispersion field with desirable properties such as positive definiteness and support on the positive real numbers domain.

Research into high-pressure mixtures of helium, hydrogen, and oxygen aims to optimize the properties of combustible gas for inertial confinement fusion studies. To achieve this goal, a $10\,{\mu}\mathrm{s}$, $10\, \mathrm{J}$ laser was directed at $0.4\,\mathrm{g}$ pressurized He, H$_2$, and O$_2$ samples, and the resulting combustion was analyzed. The study found that the energy released during combustion was consistent with data obtained through a simplified model, indicating that the energy released was primarily due to a radiative process rather than a conduction mechanism. The study also found that the energy released during combustion was influenced by the initial temperature of the gas, which in turn affects how easily the energy is released. The study found that the energy released during combustion was lower than expected, indicating that the energy released during combustion was primarily due to a radiative process rather than a conduction mechanism. The study found that the energy released during combustion was lower than expected, indicating that the energy released during combustion was primarily due to a radiative process rather than a conduction mechanism.

Deep learning techniques have revolutionized semantic segmentation tasks, but current models require extensive computational resources, limiting their practical applications. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed compact models suitable for mobile and web platforms, but often sacrificing performance. To achieve a balance between efficiency and accuracy, we propose a new boundary-aware network that leverages the relationship between segmentation and boundary maps to enhance performance on low-resource devices. Our approach is evaluated on the CamVase and CityScapes datasets and exhibits a notable improvement over the baseline, demonstrating an increase of 3.8% and 2.2% in mean IoU, especially in the fine level, without a significant increase in computational complexity.

Modern vehicles, equipped with advanced driver assistance systems, are transforming roadways, yet they still require the involvement of human drivers who must coordinate with other vehicles through nonverbal cues.  A proposed driver messenger system, consisting of driver assistants and vehicle-to-vehicle communication, aims to facilitate more efficient collaboration among drivers on the road.  By conveying intended actions through a designated messenger, other drivers on the scene can respond with their perceptions of those actions, allowing the involved drivers to synchronize their actions and maximize road safety and efficiency.  This driver messenger system is demonstrated through a lane change application, where messages are tailored to account for varying perspectives based on prior knowledge of the scene.  Through simulations, it's shown that the system's recommendations align with prior knowledge and that the risk of unsafe maneuvers is minimized when other drivers respond to the messenger's messages.

The movement of non-interacting, weakly active microorganisms in a two-dimensional environment is being examined, specifically with boundaries present. This study focuses on the effects of various boundaries on the steady-state distribution and mobility of these microorganisms. The investigation considers diverse geometric arrangements, including a flat surface, surfaces with corners, and those with concave features. The results show that boundaries have a substantial impact on the steady-state movement of these microorganisms. Notably, in a two-dimensional environment, even immobile boundaries can cause non-active particles to acquire directed motion. The research reveals that boundaries can generate non-monotonic variations in steady-state density and mobility. The findings of this study offer a deeper understanding of non-active microorganisms moving in geometric environments and may have practical applications in fields like cell biology and active matter research.

The Average Particle Model, with the addition of Siegert states, is examined within the context of describing the energy levels of nuclei. This description assumes that among states of the same energy level, there are those that are connected to the ground state of the same nucleus, referred to as Siegert states. It is demonstrated that the inclusion of Siegert states significantly improves the model's ability to accurately predict the energy levels of low-lying states in stable nuclei. This improvement results in part from the fact that the Siegert states contribute to the density of states near the ground state, thereby reducing the variance in the Gamow-Teller density. This description is supported by the inclusion of a variable parameter, with the value of this parameter being determined through analysis of the Gamow-Teller density. It is found that the value of this parameter is approximately 0.5 for stable nuclei. This result is in agreement with the findings of previous studies.

Observations of the Si IV 1398 nm line in a solar flare were made using the Interface Wide-Field Imaging (WFI) instrument onboard the International Relativistic Submillimeter Telescope.  Due to its high sensitivity, the WFI can detect the Si IV line at a cadence of one image per second, allowing for detailed analysis of the line's rapid changes.  These changes were found to be highly correlated with changes in non-thermal electron flux, suggesting a strong correlation between the line's intensity and the electron flux.  Further analysis of the line's profiles revealed a correlation between the line's intensity and the width of its core, as well as a correlation between the line's intensity and the strength of its wings.  These findings suggest that the line's intensity is primarily sensitive to the non-thermal electron flux, rather than other factors.

The strong CP problem, which is a fundamental issue in QCD, has been the subject of extensive research for nearly 30 years. This problem, which is a fundamental aspect of strong interactions, involves a CP-violating parameter, the $\theta$-term, that is expected to be extremely small. This article reviews the recent findings regarding the strong CP problem, which are primarily focused on the electric dipole moment of nucleons and is motivated by the recent discovery of the Higgs boson. It is also argued that the strong CP problem may be resolved if an approximate $Z_3$ symmetry is found, which would imply that the axion is a fundamental component of QCD.

Illuminated thin films that undergo irradiation can be etched via a non-thermal process where photons generate displaced atoms that then excavate and remove material from the film. This non-irradiation process, where atoms are removed without excess energy, is an area of interest. In this study, the factors influencing the critical angle below which non-irradiated thin films can be etched via a non-thermal process were investigated. A computational model was developed to simulate the production of displaced atoms and their movement within the film, as well as the interaction between these atoms and the film surface. This model was used to examine the effects of the spatial distribution of displaced atoms and their initial velocity vectors on the film's etching behavior. The findings indicate that the distribution of these atoms is the primary factor influencing the critical angle, and that their initial velocity vectors have a minimal impact. This conclusion was supported by comparing the model's predictions with experimental results obtained from irradiating thin SiO2 films with 20 keV Ar ions.

In computer science research, the issue of originality is a significant concern, as the lack of originality can severely impact a researcher's reputation. This paper outlines a methodology for detecting originality in source code, which is designed to identify instances where code is substantially similar without being identical. This can occur due to intentional or unintentional acts, such as plagiarism, errors, and third-party code incorporation, along with other factors. To address this issue, the paper presents a methodology that utilizes control-flow graphs to track control-flow dependencies in source code, thus eliminating variability that is often overlooked by conventional plagiarism detection techniques. This approach focuses on functional nuances by analyzing the dataflow and control-flow dependencies of methods.

We prove a full version of the Waldspurger-granville theorem for a type of polynomial-majorant polynomial minorant Dirichlet series, showing the series eventually exceed any non-negative real value in terms of absolute value. This theorem has applications in two areas: first, it resolves a conjecture made by Li for L-function families with respect to a fixed modulus; second, it further refines the known results of the "strong" Chowla conjecture as proven by Motohashi and Ivić. The proof of our theorem relies on the use of past results related to L-function estimations, specifically the bounded L^2 bound and the critical line L^2 boundedness.

Let G be a metric space, and let it be given along with a subset A of G that is almost a subgroup.  The following condition needs to be satisfied: there exists a certain number k, and for any number n greater than or equal to k, we can find a subset B subse A, and a function f that maps the set from 0 to n inclusive onto A, with the property that for any pair of numbers i and j within this range, the distance between f(i) and f(j) is at least k.  Then we can find a subgroup H of G that is isomorphic to the additive group of integers, and such that for any number n greater than or equal to k, the distance between f(i) and f(j) is at least the distance between 2 times i and 2 times j for any i and j in H.

We have developed an innovative statistical method that can accurately estimate probability distributions in various dimensions, ranging from one to several thousand. Our approach uses log-concave densities and employs a Bayesian inference technique combined with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. In contrast to the prevailing methods, our algorithm is capable of handling significantly larger data sets and higher dimensions, making it a more practical option for real-world applications. Furthermore, it is up to two orders of magnitude faster, which allows for the estimation of densities based on only 1,000 to 100,000 data points. We have evaluated the performance of our algorithm through a series of experiments on both artificially generated and real-world data, demonstrating that it can produce high-quality results that are comparable to, or even surpass those of existing techniques.

Sampling configurations of a granular packing using a Monte Carlo method can be problematic, especially when exploring the vast configuration space of a static granular system. By applying the Wang-Landau algorithm to this challenge, it is possible to efficiently map the entropy of the system onto an energy-based phase space. This approach is significant in that it enables the derivation of the entropy of a granular packing based on its volume and packing structure, allowing for the identification of specific packing modes and their corresponding entropies. Consequently, the results provide valuable insights into the structural and energetic characteristics of a granular packing and its relationship to its volume.

We introduce an innovative graphical model of cooperative co-evolutionary processes, where an explorer and a pathfinder collaborate to achieve a shared goal of fully exploring a network. The explorer relies on the pathfinder to select each subsequent location to visit, and the pathfinder earns rewards based on the explorer's location until it terminates. Our findings, derived through both theoretical analysis and computational simulation, reveal that even in complex networks with high connectivity, the pathfinder often struggles to access the largest unexplored regions. This model serves as a general framework for understanding cooperative exploration in networked systems, and we demonstrate its applicability to real-world contexts such as data analysis and autonomous navigation.

We investigate how frequencies are connected through the spectral density of a Gaussian process in a single trajectory. Our analysis reveals that, as the spectral density reaches its maximum frequency, it exhibits a sudden, discontinuous change at a specific power law for processes with fractional Brownian motion characteristics. Conversely, self-similar stationary Gaussian processes display a smooth change defined by a distinct exponent. These distinct behaviors enable the identification of an individual trajectory and its specific properties.

This paper's primary objective is to examine the interaction between (1+1)-dimensional high-order Broer-Kaup systems. To accomplish this, we utilize the Inverse Scattering Transformation technique to investigate two types of interactions: the interaction between the high-order Broer-Kaup system and the first-order Broer-Kaup system, and the high-order system's interaction with the first-order one-component shallow water equation system. The analysis yields new solutions for these combined systems.

Recently, B. Desjardins and J.-M. Schonbek demonstrated that the Euler solution with an initial velocity from the H^1(\R^3) field preserves energy. They achieved this by analyzing the decay of the L^2 norm of the vorticity. Within this study, we establish that the energy is maintained by weak solutions within the H^1(\R^3) initial condition domain. Our argument primarily focuses on the decay of the L^2 norm of the vorticity and its rotation.

The Human Brain Project's Virtual Reality initiative, VIRUP, is a pioneering project that creates immersive environments for scientific discovery and public engagement. By leveraging innovative VR technologies, VIRUP enables users to explore diverse virtual scenarios, from simulated cities to fantastical worlds inspired by Mythology and Folklore. This article outlines the Virtual Environment's design, featuring detailed case studies and user feedback, and discusses future enhancements that will shape the project's near-term evolution.

The concept of data has become increasingly prominent in recent years, yet it was not until the 1990s that it was formally recognized as an independent entity by leading data scientists. As a result, education systems have struggled to effectively integrate data studies into existing curricula, leaving students with a limited understanding of this critical concept. Our solution, Data bricks Space Voyage, addresses this gap by creating an engaging, interactive experience that enables young people to explore and understand data in a hands-on manner. This educational tool utilizes tangible objects and a customized board game to make data analysis accessible and enjoyable for kids. Our research, which involved testing the system with 27 students, revealed that this approach not only fosters a deeper understanding of data but also encourages students to think more creatively about the data they are analyzing.

In software-defined networking (SDN), the flow installation process in the data-plane is crucial for the operation of the network, and the flow installation workflow is a key factor in ensuring correct network functioning. However, the flow installation process is complex and can lead to unexpected delays and errors in the network. Our research aims to identify and track flow installation workflows in SDN data-planes, enabling the detection of anomalies and issues. We have developed a solution that uses a combination of static analysis and dynamic execution, incorporating a novel flow identification technique and a lightweight probing method to track data-plane operations. Our evaluation on four real-world and three open-source SDN controllers reveals that the solution can accurately identify and track flow installation workflows and detect various anomalies in real-world scenarios.

Recent years have seen a growing interest in disentangled representation learning. Although previous studies have made progress, they often fail to capture relational information, resulting in unsatisfactory performance in tasks that require it. To address this limitation, we propose a new perspective that disentangled representation should incorporate both instance-specific and relational representations. Our approach, RelD, utilizes variational autoencoders to learn disentangled representation and applies adversarial inference to learn a point-wise embedding that captures relational information. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function, the relational disentanglement adversarial loss, to ensure the disentanglement of instance-specific and relational representations. Experimental results demonstrate that RelD outperforms other methods in generating relational disentangled representations.

This research explores the effect of moving obstacles on energy harvesting from wake-swept foil oscillations in harmonic motion. The dynamic interaction between the moving foil and stationary foil is examined through numerical simulations. The study evaluates energy collection efficiency by analyzing power generated by both foils, with one foil positioned ahead of the other. The results show that the moving foil's amplitude and frequency increase due to the wake-swept foil's response. Conversely, the wake foil's natural frequency is lower than the upstream frequency, with a corresponding reduction in wake amplitude observed in both scenarios. However, the tandem configuration with optimal wake-foil synchronization yields higher energy collection rates than the single oscillating foil scenario.

We've developed a Bayesian method to calculate real-time quantities from lattice QCD. This method is based on Bayesian inference and involves making assumptions about the time-dependent correlation functions that minimize data assumptions. The assumed parameters are adjusted to maximize the likelihood based on the sampled data. The proposed method is applied to the time-dependent gluon propagator in a non-perturbed QCD environment, where the assumptions are tested and the accuracy of the results is evaluated. Notably, our approach is also able to produce an initial estimate of the time-dependent correlation functions.

We have developed a novel method to investigate the charge-tunneling phenomenon between a nanoscale electronic device and a built-in electrical sensor within a superconducting hybrid system. This innovative technique, which utilizes a second electrical sensor, enables us to detect the phase of the hybrid system's complex environmental interaction without disrupting the charge transfer process, effectively eliminating potential interference caused by the sensor. Utilizing this technique, we were able to gain a more accurate understanding of the hybrid system's complex environmental interaction. This is achieved by isolating the hybrid system's environmental interaction into two distinct components: the intrinsic superconducting system and the electrical sensor. This two-part interaction allows us to analyze the hybrid system's environmental interaction in greater detail. Furthermore, our research offers a new approach for studying and characterizing the hybrid system's environmental interaction. This is achieved by analyzing the electrical sensor's environmental interaction in relation to the hybrid system's environmental interaction. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our research using a hybrid system consisting of a superconducting system and an electrostatically controlled sensor. This is achieved by analyzing the hybrid system's environmental interaction and identifying the effects of the electrical sensor on the hybrid system's behavior. Our research offers a new approach for studying and characterizing the hybrid system's environmental interaction. This is achieved by analyzing the hybrid system's environmental interaction and identifying the effects of the electrical sensor on the hybrid system's behavior.

The primary goal of our research is to develop a generative model that creates new molecules with improved therapeutic properties. We introduce a pioneering generative model that uses an energy function to drive the generation of new molecules. This model is trained on two key components: a graph representation of molecules and a set of molecular descriptors. We develop two distinct energy functions to capture different aspects of the desired therapeutic properties, allowing the model to simultaneously optimize multiple characteristics. We evaluate our energy-driven model against established baselines on two datasets, demonstrating its ability to produce molecules with enhanced therapeutic properties.

The Graph Token Algorithm (GTA) is a token-driven approach to distributed system communication, which relies on tokens as discrete packets of information. Formally, GTA models are defined as graph structures incorporating token and process entities, where each node accommodates a process along with its associated token, while process interactions are based on token exchanges. In this context, the process's computational pace is dictated by token arrivals. Following a description of this framework, the concept will be applied to the evaluation of lambda-calculus, specifically within the context of the Geometry of Interaction, where lambda-calculus terms are represented as tokens and process computations as graph node operations, thus, the actual execution process can be visualized within the GDA structure, thus, the actual execution process can be visualized within the GDA structure, thus, revealing a dynamic, spatial representation of GOI computation.

The Large Magellanic Cloud is a unique astronomical object, comprising two distinct galaxies, the large LMC and the small SMC, which are gravitationally tied together. The interconnection between these two galaxies has a profound impact on their overall structure, particularly in their outer regions. To better understand the effects of SMC proximity on LMC star movement, we employed a novel approach to model the SMC's influence using a N-body simulation. The resulting model enabled us to simulate the effects of SMC stars and dark matter on LMC star movement, which we applied to the data from the VMC survey. Our analysis revealed that the SMC's presence significantly affects LMC star movement, particularly in its outer regions, with stars moving away from the center at a rate of 0.3 to 0.5 mas/yr. We also observed a notable increase in the number of stars moving towards the center in the bar region, particularly in the south-east area. Our findings have important implications for the future analysis of LMC star movement, particularly in its outer regions.

The detection of power theft in smart grid systems using automated metering infrastructure is a pressing concern due to its impact on both the utility and the consumer. Recent studies have shown that deep learning techniques are particularly effective in identifying the issue. Nonetheless, selecting the optimal deep learning model and its parameters poses significant challenges. This paper proposes a novel approach to address these challenges by developing a deep learning model that can automatically select the best architecture and parameters for power theft detection using a random search method. This method utilizes a recurrent neural network and applies a combination of convolutional and recurrent layers to extract meaningful features from smart meter consumption data. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach over existing methods.

Compact graphs defined on a two-dimensional manifold with no isolated vertices are called surface graphs. A construction is developed that allows for the creation of any surface graph by combining or removing edges from a compact surface, and also permits the creation of any surface graph by removing edges from a compact covering space of the complex plane. This is used to show that any surface graph can be approximated by a compact graph by successively adding edges, which leads to the solution of the topological edge recognition problem on surface graphs. The problem of recognizing edges on surface graphs is found to be equivalent to the problem of testing the membership of edges in certain compact graphs.

Using a massive dataset of $pp$ collisions gathered by the LHCb experiment at 13 TeV, we have measured the lifetimes of the baryons $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$. The baryons were created through the process $p$ + $p$ $\rightarrow$ $\Xi^{-}$ $K^{+}$ $K^{-}$ $K^{-}$, and their decay modes were identified via the distinctive decay process $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ $\rightarrow$ $\Xi^{-}$ $K^{-}$ $\pi^{+}$ $\pi^{-}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$.
